claim: PLB-985 cells differentiate into neutrophil-like cells that resemble primary human neutrophils in various ways.
source: PLB-985 differentiate into neutrophil-like cells that resemble primary human neutrophils in various ways (Zhen et al., 1993; Pedruzzi et al., 2002; Pivot-Pajot et al., 2010; Marin-Esteban et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature demonstrating the similarity between PLB-985 and primary neutrophils.

claim: PLB-985 cells change their nuclear morphology and develop granules throughout 7 days of differentiation.
source: PLB-985 changed their nuclear morphology and developed granules, though fewer than primary neutrophils, throughout the 7 days of differentiation (referred as d0 to d7 in this report) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1a demonstrating morphological changes.

claim: Differentiated PLB-985 cells produce ROS in response to PMA.
source: Once differentiated, PLB-985 also produced ROS in response to the agonist phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a measuring ROS production.

claim: Differentiated PLB-985 cells upregulate the surface marker CD11b.
source: Once differentiated, PLB-985 also produced ROS in response to the agonist phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) and upregulated the surface marker CD11b (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1c demonstrating CD11b upregulation.

claim: Differentiated PLB-985 cells phagocytose Escherichia coli.
source: Furthermore, differentiated PLB-985 phagocytosed Escherichia coli, a process that could be blocked by the phagocytosis inhibitor cytochalasin B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b demonstrating phagocytosis of E. coli.

claim: PMA induces cell death in fully differentiated PLB-985 but not in d0 or d3 cells.
source: Importantly, PMA potently induced cell death in fully differentiated PLB-985, but not in d0 or d3 cells (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d measuring cell death over time.

claim: PMA-induced cell death in PLB-985 is morphologically similar to NETosis.
source: PMA-induced cell death was morphologically similar to NETosis; dying PLB-985 expanded their nuclei and a significant fraction released DNA as shown by SYTOX Green staining (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images and SYTOX Green staining data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The calcium ionophore A23187 induces cell death in PLB-985 at both d3 and d7 of differentiation.
source: Of note, the calcium ionophore A23187, another stimulant of NET formation, also induced cell death in PLB-985, both at d3 and d7 of differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d measuring cell death in response to A23187.

claim: NOX2-deficient PLB-985 cells fail to produce an oxidative burst in response to PMA.
source: Differentiated PLB-985 cells lacking NOX2 failed to produce an oxidative burst and did not undergo cell death in response to PMA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f demonstrating lack of ROS production in NOX2-deficient cells.

claim: NOX2-deficient PLB-985 cells do not undergo cell death in response to PMA.
source: Differentiated PLB-985 cells lacking NOX2 failed to produce an oxidative burst and did not undergo cell death in response to PMA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f demonstrating lack of cell death in NOX2-deficient cells.

claim: NCF2-deficient PLB-985 cells do not die upon PMA stimulation.
source: To inactivate NADPH oxidase independently of NOX2, we also disrupted expression of its NCF2 subunit, and showed again that these cells did not die upon PMA stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g demonstrating lack of cell death in NCF2-deficient cells.

claim: PMA-induced NET formation requires full differentiation of PLB-985 cells.
source: We found that PMA-induced NET formation required full differentiation of PLB-985.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PMA induces cell death only in fully differentiated PLB-985 cells (d7) but not in d0 or d3 cells.

claim: CYBB, NCF1, and MPO were identified as hits in the genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen.
source: Underlining the validity of the screening approach, we identified CYBB, NCF1 and MPO as hits; all three are known to be required for PMA-induced NET formation (Fuchs et al., 2007; Metzler et al., 2011; Figure 1g, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by screen results shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—source data 1, and validated by citations showing these genes are required for NET formation.

claim: CEBPD was identified as a hit in the genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen.
source: We also found CEBPD, a member of the C/EBP family of transcription factors that are crucial for granulopoiesis (Wang and Friedman, 2002; Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by screen results shown in Figure 1g and citation indicating CEBPD's role in granulopoiesis.

claim: HIST1H1E (H1.4) was identified as a hit in the genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screen with 100% of sgRNAs overrepresented and the highest median enrichment.
source: HIST1H1E (H1.4) was overrepresented with 100% of sgRNAs and showed the highest median enrichment (Figure 1g, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by screen results shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: There are five somatic replication-dependent H1 subtypes (H1.1 – H1.5) and two replication-independent H1 subtypes (H1.0 and H1X).
source: There are five somatic replication-dependent (H1.1 – H1.5) and two replication-independent H1 subtypes (H1.0 and H1X).
evidence: This is established knowledge about H1 histone subtypes.

claim: PLB-985 cells express H1.2 and H1.4 mRNA more abundantly than other H1 subtypes.
source: PLB-985 expressed mRNA encoding H1.2 and H1.4 more abundantly than the other subtypes (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2a measuring mRNA expression levels.

claim: Expression of replication-dependent H1 subtypes occurs mainly in the S phase of proliferating cells.
source: The expression of replication-dependent H1 subtypes occurs mainly in the S phase of proliferating cells and, accordingly, H1 mRNA levels decreased during PLB-985 differentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, same experiments as in Figure 2a, but plotted as relative to d0).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about replication-dependent histones and experimental data showing decreased mRNA during differentiation.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4 protein levels decrease as PLB-985 cells mature.
source: When we looked at H1.2 and H1.4 protein expression of PLB-985 during differentiation, we found that protein levels also decreased as the cells matured (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Human primary neutrophils express H1.2 and H1.4 as the most abundantly expressed H1 subtypes.
source: Accordingly, human primary neutrophils isolated from blood of healthy donors expressed detectable amounts of the H1 genes. H1.2 and H1.4, the two hits in our genome wide screen, were the most abundantly expressed subtypes (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from primary neutrophils shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Cell death is reduced in H1.2-deficient PLB-985 clones in response to PMA.
source: Cell death was reduced in both H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones, confirming the results of the screen (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c measuring cell death in H1.2-deficient clones.

claim: Cell death is reduced in H1.4-deficient PLB-985 clones in response to PMA.
source: Cell death was reduced in both H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones, confirming the results of the screen (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c measuring cell death in H1.4-deficient clones.

claim: H1.2-deficient PLB-985 clones produce ROS less efficiently than wild type cells upon PMA stimulation.
source: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones produced ROS less efficiently than wild type cells upon PMA stimulation (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d measuring ROS production.

claim: H1.4-deficient PLB-985 clones produce ROS less efficiently than wild type cells upon PMA stimulation.
source: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones produced ROS less efficiently than wild type cells upon PMA stimulation (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d measuring ROS production.

claim: Cells deficient for H1.2 or H1.4 express less MPO.
source: Furthermore, cells deficient for either of the two H1 subtypes expressed less MPO (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2e demonstrating reduced MPO expression.

claim: Cells deficient for H1.2 or H1.4 can still phagocytose.
source: Cells deficient for H1.2 or H1.4 could still phagocytose, demonstrating that not all effector functions were equally affected by the loss of H1 subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g,h).
evidence: Supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g,h.

claim: Deficiency of H1.2 and H1.4 affects PLB-985 maturation.
source: These findings suggest that H1.2 and H1.4 are required for PLB-985 to differentiate into mature, neutrophil-like cells.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including reduced ROS production, reduced MPO expression, and reduced cell death in response to PMA.

claim: Surface expression of CD11b is decreased in H1.2-deficient cells at d3 and d7 of differentiation.
source: To confirm that deficiency of H1.2 and H1.4 affected PLB-985 maturation, we showed that surface expression of the differentiation marker CD11b is decreased on both d3 and d7 of differentiation (Figure 3a,b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b) in cells where these genes were deleted.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3a,b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Surface expression of CD11b is decreased in H1.4-deficient cells at d3 and d7 of differentiation.
source: To confirm that deficiency of H1.2 and H1.4 affected PLB-985 maturation, we showed that surface expression of the differentiation marker CD11b is decreased on both d3 and d7 of differentiation (Figure 3a,b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b) in cells where these genes were deleted.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3a,b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Loss of H1.1, H1.3, and H1.5 results in enhanced expression of CD11b at d3 of differentiation.
source: We observed markedly enhanced expression of CD11b already at d3, especially in clones deficient in H1.1 and H1.5 (Figure 3a,b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3a,b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Loss of H1 subtypes does not generally impact myelopoiesis or innate immune functions in THP-1 cells.
source: To test whether these effects were specific to neutrophilic cells, we also disrupted expression of H1 subtypes in the monocytic cell line THP-1 and analyzed their ability to release IL-1β via the NLRP3 inflammasome. Batch populations of H1-deficient cells released similar amounts of IL-1β than control cells when activated with silica crystals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c). We therefore conclude that loss of H1 subtypes does not generally impact myelopoiesis or innate immune functions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c demonstrating similar IL-1β release in H1-deficient THP-1 cells.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 clones grow unrestrictedly until d7 of differentiation.
source: Interestingly, H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones grew unrestrictedly until d7, whereas cells deficient in H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 decreased in comparison to controls (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Cells deficient in H1.1, H1.3, and H1.5 show decreased growth compared to controls during differentiation.
source: Interestingly, H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones grew unrestrictedly until d7, whereas cells deficient in H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 decreased in comparison to controls (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells are more viable than controls at d8 and d12 of differentiation.
source: In line with their enhanced growth, H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells were more viable than controls, whereas H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5-deficient cells showed less viability than controls (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: H1.1, H1.3, and H1.5-deficient cells show less viability than controls at d8 and d12 of differentiation.
source: In line with their enhanced growth, H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells were more viable than controls, whereas H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5-deficient cells showed less viability than controls (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: Supported by viability data shown in Figure 3e,f.

claim: Cells deficient in H1.1 have a stronger oxidative burst in response to PMA than control cells.
source: Of note, cells deficient in H1.1 had a stronger oxidative burst in response to PMA than control cells, consistent with enhanced maturation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Clones deficient in H1.3 and H1.5 produce less ROS than control cells in response to PMA.
source: Clones deficient in H1.3 and H1.5, on the other hand, produced less ROS than control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: PLB-985 and primary human neutrophils concordantly regulate processes during differentiation.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated that PLB-985 and primary cells concordantly regulate processes during differentiation (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b. Figure 4—figure supplement 1a depicts the same analysis as Figure 4a with the gene set labels).
evidence: Supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing PLB-985 and primary cells shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: PLB-985 and primary cells follow a similar differentiation trajectory.
source: Using principal component analysis (PCA), we saw that these cells follow a similar differentiation trajectory (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c comparing PLB-985 and primary cells.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones at d7 cluster more closely with control cells at d3, indicating delayed differentiation.
source: We analyzed the H1-deficient clones by PCA and found that H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones at d7 clustered more closely with control cells at d3, indicating delayed differentiation (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: H1.1, H1.3, and H1.5-deficient cells at d3 cluster with control cells at d7, suggesting accelerated differentiation.
source: H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5-deficient cells at d3 clustered with control cells at d7, suggesting accelerated differentiation (Figure 4c).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: During differentiation, control PLB-985 cells upregulate genes related to the innate immune response and downregulate genes corresponding to cell cycle and division.
source: Analysis of the enrichment of gene modules confirmed that, during differentiation, control cells upregulated genes related to the innate immune response and downregulated genes corresponding to cell cycle and division, in line with the context of terminal differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by gene module enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: In H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells, gene modules related to differentiation are less regulated, demonstrating prolonged proliferation and obstruction of differentiation.
source: Interestingly, in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells, the modules were less regulated, again demonstrating prolonged proliferation and obstruction of differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by gene module enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells downregulate neutrophil genes such as MPO and neutrophil proteases at d0.
source: We found that both H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells downregulated neutrophil genes, such as MPO and neutrophil proteases among others (Figure 4d), indicating that lineage fate was affected in undifferentiated cells.
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4d.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells upregulate genes associated with eosinophils and a GATA-1 signature at d0.
source: Surprisingly, among the upregulated genes we found a significant number of genes associated with eosinophils and a GATA-1 signature (Figure 4d,e, see Materials and methods section for the source of datasets).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis and gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4d,e.

claim: Loss of H1.2 and H1.4 affects lineage determination of PLB-985 cells before the onset of differentiation by driving them towards a more eosinophil-like fate.
source: This suggests that loss of H1.2 and H1.4 affects lineage determination of PLB-985 cells even before the onset of differentiation by driving them towards a more eosinophil-like fate.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells upregulate eosinophil genes and downregulate neutrophil genes at d0.

claim: CEBPA is downregulated in cells deficient for H1.2 and H1.4 at d0.
source: We found downregulation of CEBPA in cells deficient for H1.2 and H1.4 at d0, but upregulation of the same transcription factors in cells deficient for H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: CEBPA is upregulated in cells deficient for H1.1, H1.3, and H1.5 at d0.
source: We found downregulation of CEBPA in cells deficient for H1.2 and H1.4 at d0, but upregulation of the same transcription factors in cells deficient for H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to enhanced expression of the eosinophil marker Siglec-8 on the surface of a subset of PLB-985 cells.
source: However, loss of H1.2 and H1.4 led to enhanced expression of the eosinophil marker Siglec-8 on the surface of a subset of PLB-985 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3b.

claim: H1.2- and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 cells express higher levels of the eosinophil protein galectin-10/CLC.
source: H1.2- and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 also expressed higher levels of the eosinophil protein galectin-10/CLC, in line of what we had seen by RNA-seq (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c,d).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3c,d.

claim: Human primary eosinophils express very high levels of H1.2 and H1.4 mRNA.
source: We also looked at H1 mRNA expression levels in human primary eosinophils and found that these cells expressed very high levels of H1.2 and H1.4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from primary eosinophils shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3e.

claim: Eosinophils express high levels of H1 subtypes according to proteomics data.
source: A proteomics dataset of cells in circulation confirmed high expression levels of H1 subtypes in eosinophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 3f; Rieckmann et al., 2017), suggesting that eosinophil maturation relies on an appropriate amount of H1 subtype expression during differentiation.
evidence: Supported by proteomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3f and citation to Rieckmann et al., 2017.

claim: The profile of circulating lymphocytes and monocytes in the blood or bone marrow of adult H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice is indistinguishable from wild type animals.
source: The profile of circulating lymphocytes and monocytes in the blood or bone marrow of adult animals was indistinguishable from wild type animals (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Wild type and H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals have the same proportion of neutrophils in circulation and in bone marrow.
source: Furthermore, wild type and H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals had the same proportion of neutrophils in circulation and in bone marrow (Figure 5a,b, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5a,b and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals have enhanced amounts of circulating eosinophils during homeostasis.
source: Importantly, although the number of eosinophils in the bone marrow were similar between genotypes (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a), H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals had enhanced amounts of circulating eosinophils during homeostasis, suggesting that, in vivo, there is also bias towards eosinophils (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice show disturbances in neutrophil ageing markers.
source: In addition to a change in eosinophil numbers in circulation, H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice showed disturbances in neutrophil ageing markers (Zhang et al., 2015; Adrover et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2015 and Adrover et al., 2019, and experimental data on CD62L and CXCR4 expression.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice have a slightly lower number of CD62L+ CXCR4- 'young' neutrophils during homeostasis.
source: We found similar expression of CD62L in bone marrow neutrophils during homeostasis, but a slightly lower number of CD62L+ CXCR4- 'young' neutrophils (Zhang et al., 2015; Adrover et al., 2019) in H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 5a–c,g).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5a–c,g and citations to Zhang et al., 2015 and Adrover et al., 2019.

claim: Upon casein injection, H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals have more CD62L+ but also more CXCR4+ neutrophils than wildtype animals.
source: Upon casein injection, we found more CD62L+, but also more CXCR4+ neutrophils in wildtype than in H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 5d–f,h).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5d–f,h.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells express enhanced levels of the chemokine CXCL1.
source: Interestingly, we also found altered expression of cytokines and chemokines. H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells expressed enhanced levels of the chemokine CXCL1, reduced amounts of IL6 mRNA, and we also found enhanced levels of IL-17 upon casein injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells express reduced amounts of IL6 mRNA.
source: Interestingly, we also found altered expression of cytokines and chemokines. H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells expressed enhanced levels of the chemokine CXCL1, reduced amounts of IL6 mRNA, and we also found enhanced levels of IL-17 upon casein injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals have enhanced levels of IL-17 upon casein injection.
source: Interestingly, we also found altered expression of cytokines and chemokines. H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells expressed enhanced levels of the chemokine CXCL1, reduced amounts of IL6 mRNA, and we also found enhanced levels of IL-17 upon casein injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6a–d.

claim: The response of bone marrow cells to G-CSF is altered upon loss of H1.2/H1.4; these cells are more viable after overnight incubation in the presence of G-CSF than wild type cells.
source: However, the response of bone marrow cells to G-CSF was altered upon loss of H1.2/H1.4; these cells were more viable after overnight incubation in the presence of G-CSF than wild type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 7a).
evidence: Supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7a.

claim: Bone marrow cells of H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice are more granular than wild type cells.
source: Furthermore, bone marrow cells of H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice were more granular than wild type cells, which could reflect reduced spontaneous degranulation or differentially aged cells (Adrover et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 7b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7b and citation to Adrover et al., 2020.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient neutrophils are more granular in the bone marrow during homeostasis and upon casein injection, but not in circulation.
source: We also looked at the granularity of neutrophils in circulation and in the bone marrow of animals during homeostatic and inflammatory conditions. H1.2/H1.4-deficient neutrophils were more granular in the bone marrow, both during homeostasis and upon casein injection, but not in circulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 7c,d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7c,d.

claim: H1.2/H1.4-deficient hematopoietic stem cells express elevated levels of surface markers for eosinophils and decreased levels of neutrophil surface markers compared to wild type cells.
source: Importantly, H1.2/H1.4-deficient cells expressed elevated levels of surface markers for eosinophils and decreased levels of neutrophil surface markers, as compared to wild type cells. This recapitulates the phenotype we observed in PLB-985 (Figure 5d–f).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from ex vivo differentiated bone marrow cells shown in Figure 5d–f.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4 cooperate to determine the neutrophil-eosinophil cell fate decision in hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: These experiments show that H1.2 and H1.4 cooperate to determine the neutrophil-eosinophil cell fate decision in hematopoietic progenitor cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1.2/H1.4-deficient cells show enhanced eosinophil differentiation and reduced neutrophil differentiation both in PLB-985 and in murine hematopoietic stem cells.

claim: GATA-1 and GATA-2 were upregulated on mRNA level in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout PLB-985 lines.
source: Two transcription factors required for eosinophil differentiation, GATA-1 and GATA-2, were upregulated on mRNA level in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout lines (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: GATA2 transcripts are higher than GATA1 in PLB-985 cells.
source: GATA2 transcripts were higher than GATA1 and transcript levels of both transcription factors at d0 inversely correlated with the potential of PLB-985 to adopt a neutrophil-like cell fate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: In mice, GATA1 mRNA expression is higher than GATA2.
source: Interestingly, in mice GATA1 mRNA expression was higher than GATA2, and we could also see enhanced expression of GATA1 in H1.2/H1.4-deficient bone marrow cells as compared to wild type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from murine bone marrow shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Expression of GATA2 does not change in H1.2/H1.4-deficient murine bone marrow cells.
source: Expression of GATA2 did not change in H1.2/H1.4-deficient murine cells, but we saw a slight downregulation of CEBPA, which is in line with the expression profiles of PLB-985 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from murine bone marrow shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: CEBPA is slightly downregulated in H1.2/H1.4-deficient murine bone marrow cells.
source: Expression of GATA2 did not change in H1.2/H1.4-deficient murine cells, but we saw a slight downregulation of CEBPA, which is in line with the expression profiles of PLB-985 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data from murine bone marrow shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d,e.

claim: GATA-2 deficiency enhances maturation of PLB-985 cells.
source: Interestingly, GATA-2 deficiency enhanced maturation of PLB-985, as indicated by an increased ability to produce ROS in response to PMA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: GATA-1 knockout PLB-985 lines behave as scrambled control cells.
source: In contrast, GATA-1 knockout lines behaved as scr. cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Disruption of GATA-2 expression rescues ROS production in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 cells.
source: Importantly, disruption of GATA-2 expression rescued ROS production (Figure 6a–c) and CD11b expression (Figure 6d) in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985.
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 6a–c.

claim: Disruption of GATA-2 expression rescues CD11b expression in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 cells.
source: Importantly, disruption of GATA-2 expression rescued ROS production (Figure 6a–c) and CD11b expression (Figure 6d) in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Disruption of GATA-1 has no effect on rescuing the differentiation phenotype of H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 cells.
source: Again, disruption of GATA-1 had no effect (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by ROS production and CD11b expression data shown in Figure 6a–d.

claim: Loss of GATA-2 is sufficient to allow differentiation in the absence of H1.2 and H1.4.
source: These experiments demonstrate that the differentiation phenotype resulting from H1.2 and H1.4 deficiency depends on upregulation of GATA-2 and, importantly, that loss of GATA-2 is sufficient to allow differentiation in the absence of these H1 subtypes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA-2 deficiency rescues the differentiation defects in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells.

claim: Inhibition of GATA-2 enhances CD11b expression of H1.2 or H1.4-deficient PLB-985 lines.
source: Inhibition of GATA-2 enhanced CD11b expression of H1.2 or H1.4-deficient lines (Figure 6e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6e.

claim: GATA-2 inhibition upregulates expression of AQP9 in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout lines at d7 of differentiation.
source: GATA-2 inhibition upregulated expression of AQP9 and downregulated expression of MPO in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout lines at d7 of differentiation, indicating a rescue of maturation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,c.

claim: GATA-2 inhibition downregulates expression of MPO in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout lines at d7 of differentiation.
source: GATA-2 inhibition upregulated expression of AQP9 and downregulated expression of MPO in H1.2 and H1.4 knockout lines at d7 of differentiation, indicating a rescue of maturation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b,c.

claim: GATA-2 inhibition restores the capacity of H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones to mount an oxidative burst.
source: In line with our results with CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene disruption, GATA-2 inhibition restored the capacity of H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones to mount an oxidative burst (Figure 6f–h).
evidence: Supported by ROS production data shown in Figure 6f–h.

claim: Treatment with the GATA-1 inhibitor does not affect maturation and function of PLB-985 of any genotype.
source: As expected, treatment with the GATA-1 inhibitor did not affect maturation and function of PLB-985 of either genotype (Figure 6e,i–k).
evidence: Supported by CD11b expression and ROS production data shown in Figure 6e,i–k.

claim: The combination of GATA-1 and GATA-2 inhibitors does not have an additive effect on PLB-985 maturation.
source: The combination of GATA-1 and GATA-2 inhibitors did not have an additive effect on PLB-985 maturation, confirming that GATA-2 is the relevant transcription factor for the phenotype observed in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient clones in the human cell system (Figure 6—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Supported by CD11b expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2d.

claim: The response to either GATA-2 deficiency or inhibition is stronger in H1-deficient PLB-985 than in scrambled control cells.
source: Importantly, the response to either GATA-2 deficiency or inhibition was stronger in H1-deficient PLB-985 than in scr. cells. This is in line with enhanced baseline expression of the transcription factor in H1.2 or H1.4-deficient clones.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA-2 deficiency or inhibition has a greater effect on H1-deficient cells, which have higher baseline GATA-2 expression.

claim: H1.2 and H1.4 affect fate determination and subsequent neutrophil differentiation and function at least partly through the regulation of GATA-2.
source: These data show that H1.2 and H1.4 affect fate determination and subsequent neutrophil differentiation and function at least partly through the regulation of GATA-2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA-2 deficiency or inhibition rescues the differentiation defects in H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells.

claim: Loss of H1.2 and H1.4 inhibits neutrophil differentiation while deficiency in H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 enhances it.
source: We identified an unexpected role of H1 subtypes in neutrophil development; loss of H1.2 and H1.4 inhibits differentiation while deficiency in H1.1, H1.3 and H1.5 enhances it.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental observations including CD11b expression, ROS production, cell growth, and viability data.

claim: In neutrophil precursors, H1 subtypes control the expression or activity of GATA-2, which determines cell fate via transcription of neutrophil or eosinophil-specific genes.
source: We propose that in neutrophil precursors, H1 subtypes control the expression or activity of GATA-2, which determines cell fate via transcription of neutrophil or eosinophil-specific genes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observation that H1.2 and H1.4 deficiency leads to GATA-2 upregulation and eosinophil gene expression.

claim: Enhanced expression of eosinophil genes or reduced expression of neutrophil-specific genes disrupts normal maturation, leading to prolonged proliferation and viability and reduced neutrophil function.
source: Enhanced expression of eosinophil genes – or reduced expression of neutrophil-specific genes – disrupts normal maturation, leading to prolonged proliferation and viability and reduced neutrophil function.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1.2 and H1.4-deficient cells show enhanced eosinophil gene expression, reduced neutrophil gene expression, prolonged proliferation, enhanced viability, and reduced neutrophil function.

claim: Overexpression of GATA-2 in murine progenitor cells switches their lineage determination from macrophages to a megakaryocyte state.
source: Interestingly, another study found that overexpression of GATA-2 in murine progenitor cells switched their lineage determination from macrophages to a megakaryocyte state (Kitajima et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kitajima et al., 2002.

claim: GATA-2 acts as a key molecule for fate determination of immune cells.
source: GATA-2 therefore acts as a key molecule for fate determination of immune cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA-2 affects lineage determination in multiple contexts.

claim: Enforced expression of both GATA-1 and GATA-2 can induce eosinophil differentiation of human CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Enforced expression of both GATA-1 and GATA-2 can induce eosinophil differentiation of human CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells (Hirasawa et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hirasawa et al., 2002.

claim: In murine cells, the eosinophil-promoting effect of GATA-2 depends strongly on the presence of C/EBP-α.
source: Interestingly, another study in murine cells showed that the eosinophil-promoting effect of GATA-2 depends strongly on the presence of C/EBP-α. Enforced expression of GATA-2 drove C/EBP-α expressing precursor cells into the eosinophil lineage. However, in the absence of C/EBP-α, overexpression of GATA-2 induced mast cell and basophil development (Iwasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iwasaki et al., 2006.

claim: Not only the expression levels of hematopoietic transcription factors, but also the order of their expression is crucial for lineage determination.
source: Therefore, not only the expression levels of hematopoietic transcription factors, but also the order of their expression is crucial for lineage determination.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GATA-2 has different effects depending on the presence or absence of C/EBP-α.

claim: PLB-985 cells express C/EBP-α in the undifferentiated state.
source: PLB-985 express C/EBP-α in the undifferentiated state, and enhanced expression of GATA-2 can therefore explain the upregulation of eosinophil markers we found in our experiments using this cell line.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-seq data showing C/EBP-α expression in PLB-985 cells.

claim: Adult H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals have normal numbers of circulating neutrophils.
source: However, adult H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals had normal numbers of circulating neutrophils, indicating that neutrophil differentiation is compensated.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing similar neutrophil numbers in wild type and H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.

claim: The turnover rate or the longevity of neutrophils is affected in H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly the turnover rate or the longevity of neutrophils seemed to be affected in these mice, since we found reduced amounts of young neutrophils in H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced CD62L+ CXCR4- 'young' neutrophils in H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.

claim: Neutrophils isolated from H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals show enhanced granularity and longevity.
source: We also found enhanced granularity and longevity of neutrophils isolated from H1.2/H1.4-deficient animals.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing enhanced granularity and viability assay data showing enhanced longevity.

claim: Neutropenia in peripheral tissues triggers de novo production of neutrophils in the bone marrow.
source: Neutropenia in peripheral tissues triggers de novo production of neutrophils in the bone marrow (Stark et al., 2005), demonstrating that granulopoiesis in vivo is regulated by feedback loops.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stark et al., 2005.

claim: Initial neutrophil deficiency in adult H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice is compensated by a different cytokine milieu.
source: This suggests that initial neutrophil deficiency in adult H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice is compensated by a different cytokine milieu.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of altered cytokine expression and normal neutrophil numbers in H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.

claim: In human breast cancer cells, combined loss of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to an upregulation of an interferon signature.
source: Interestingly, in human breast cancer cells, combined loss of H1.2 and H1.4 leads to an upregulation of an interferon signature (Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Izquierdo-Bouldstridge et al., 2017.

claim: H1 can act in redundant and subtype-specific ways.
source: H1 can act in redundant and subtype-specific ways (Hergeth and Schneider, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hergeth and Schneider, 2015.

claim: Mice lacking one or two H1 subtypes are viable and fertile.
source: Mice lacking one or two H1 subtypes are viable and fertile (Fan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2003.

claim: PLB-985 deficient in any of the five H1 subtypes are viable and do not show growth defects.
source: Analogously, PLB-985 deficient in any of the five H1 subtypes that we disrupted were viable and did not show growth defects.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations of viable H1-deficient PLB-985 clones.

claim: shRNA-mediated knock down of H1.2 and H1.4 reduces cell growth and viability in various non-immune cell lines.
source: This is in contrast to another study, where shRNA-mediated knock down of H1.2 and H1.4 reduced cell growth and viability in various non-immune cell lines (Sancho et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sancho et al., 2008.

claim: Loss of H1.2 and H1.4, in the context of neutrophil differentiation, enhances viability.
source: We found that loss of H1.2 and H1.4, in the context of neutrophil differentiation, enhanced viability, demonstrating cell type specific effects of H1 subtypes.
evidence: Supported by viability data showing enhanced viability of H1.2 and H1.4-deficient PLB-985 cells.

claim: H1 has long been considered a general repressor of transcription.
source: H1 has long been considered a general repressor of transcription (Schlissel and Brown, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schlissel and Brown, 1984.

claim: Genomic regions associated with active transcription are devoid of H1 subtypes in human cells.
source: Accordingly, a study in human cells found that genomic regions associated with active transcription were devoid of H1 subtypes (Izzo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Izzo et al., 2013.

claim: Murine embryonic stem cells that are triple-deficient in H1.2, H1.3 and H1.4 show only 38 differentially expressed genes when compared to wild type cells.
source: However, murine embryonic stem cells that are triple-deficient in H1.2, H1.3 and H1.4 show a surprisingly low number of only 38 differentially expressed genes when compared to wild type cells (Fan et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2005.

claim: Loss of H1 subtypes in more differentiated cells affects the expression of many genes with clear functional consequences.
source: Our data show that loss of H1 subtypes in more differentiated cells affects the expression of many genes with clear functional consequences.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing many differentially expressed genes in H1-deficient PLB-985 cells.

claim: Only a fraction of differentially expressed genes in PLB-985 is directly regulated by H1 subtypes.
source: We postulate that only a fraction of differentially expressed genes in PLB-985 is directly regulated by H1 subtypes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that H1 deficiency leads to changes in transcription factors, which then affect many downstream genes.

claim: The enhanced expression of lineage-determining transcription factors, such as GATA-2, leads to further changes in the transcriptome and affects cell differentiation.
source: The enhanced expression of lineage-determining transcription factors, such as GATA-2, leads to further changes in the transcriptome and affects cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1 deficiency leads to GATA-2 upregulation, which then affects many downstream genes and cell differentiation.

claim: H1 subtypes may directly occupy the promoter or enhancer elements of GATA2 and silence its expression.
source: It is possible that H1 subtypes directly occupy the promoter or enhancer elements of GATA2 and silence its expression.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism by which H1 subtypes regulate GATA-2 expression.

claim: H1 subtype-specific binding to genomic regions has been shown for human H1.5.
source: H1 subtype-specific binding to genomic regions has, for example, been shown for human H1.5 (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: H1.5 targets over 20-fold more regions in differentiated human lung fibroblasts than in embryonic stem cells.
source: Interestingly, H1.5 targeted over 20-fold more regions in differentiated human lung fibroblasts than in embryonic stem cells and H1.5 binding led to chromatin compaction and gene silencing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: H1.5 binding to chromatin is associated with an enrichment of demethylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3K9me2).
source: In addition to a direct repressive effect of H1.5, its binding to chromatin was also associated with an enrichment of demethylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3K9me2) (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: H3K9me2 is a posttranslational modification of a core histone that is associated with a repressive chromatin state.
source: H3K9me2 is a posttranslational modification of a core histone that is associated with a repressive chromatin state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications.

claim: H1 subtypes are likely to regulate transcription via epigenetic marks on core histones.
source: H1 subtypes are therefore likely to regulate transcription via epigenetic marks on core histones.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1.5 binding is associated with H3K9me2.

claim: H1 subtypes are posttranslationally modified in a subtype-specific manner.
source: Furthermore, H1 subtypes themselves are posttranslationally modified in a subtype-specific manner (Hergeth and Schneider, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hergeth and Schneider, 2015.

claim: H1 modifications can determine subtype-specific protein-protein interactions, chromatin binding properties or other features that subsequently cause transcriptional changes.
source: Although less is known about H1 modifications than about core histones, it is likely that such modifications can determine subtype-specific protein-protein interactions, chromatin binding properties or other features that subsequently cause transcriptional changes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequences of H1 modifications.

claim: Vertebrates express many different H1 subtypes.
source: It is puzzling that vertebrates express so many different H1 subtypes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H1 histone subtypes in vertebrates.

claim: H1 subtypes can compensate each other in extreme situations, such as the loss of one or even two subtypes in a whole organism.
source: Although they are able to compensate each other in 'extreme' situations, such as the loss of one or even two subtypes in a whole organism (Fan et al., 2003), they may also have more subtle and specific functions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Fan et al., 2003.

claim: Different H1 subtypes initiate distinct transcriptional programs.
source: This study contributes to our understanding of how different H1 subtypes initiate distinct transcriptional programs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different H1 subtypes have opposing effects on neutrophil differentiation and gene expression.

claim: The transcriptional programs initiated by H1 subtypes appear to be evolutionarily conserved.
source: Importantly, these programs appear to be evolutionarily conserved, since we found similar responses in human and murine cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1.2 and H1.4 deficiency has similar effects in human PLB-985 cells and murine hematopoietic stem cells.

claim: The number of eosinophils in bone marrow is the same between wild type and H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, eosinophil numbers in bone marrow were the same between genotypes.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing similar eosinophil numbers in bone marrow of wild type and H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice.

claim: H1 subtype regulation in vivo is subject to compensatory mechanisms that eventually adjust the levels of neutrophils.
source: Taking all these observations and limitations together, we propose that H1 subtype regulation in vivo is subject to compensatory mechanisms that eventually adjust the levels of neutrophils.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observation that H1.2/H1.4-deficient mice have normal neutrophil numbers despite defects in neutrophil differentiation.

claim: Deletion of 2 out of 5 H1 subtypes, that probably affect the epigenetic regulation of development, are subject to systemic adjustments.
source: Indeed, it is expected that deletion of 2 out of 5 H1 subtypes, that probably affect the epigenetic regulation of development, are subject to systemic adjustments.
evidence: This is a speculation about the systemic response to H1 deficiency.

claim: H1 subtypes affect the lineage determination between neutrophils and eosinophils.
source: In summary, we identified novel and opposing functions for specific H1 subtypes in granulopoiesis. H1 subtypes affect the lineage determination between neutrophils and eosinophils.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental observations showing that H1.2 and H1.4 deficiency leads to enhanced eosinophil differentiation and reduced neutrophil differentiation.

claim: Inappropriate expression of H1 subtypes in the hematopoietic compartment may shape pathologies with neutrophil or eosinophil involvement, such as asthma.
source: We speculate that inappropriate expression of H1 subtypes in the hematopoietic compartment shapes pathologies with neutrophil or eosinophil involvement, such as asthma.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical relevance of H1 subtypes in disease.

claim: Linker histones represent another layer of complexity to the process of immune cell differentiation.
source: Our findings suggest that linker histones represent another layer of complexity to the fascinating process of immune cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H1 subtypes affect immune cell differentiation in subtype-specific ways.
